### `capacity_per_week`

How much this supplier can ship per week, across everything they supply. NULL means UNLIMITED — an infinite supplier, which is a deliberate modelling choice and not a missing value.

| | |
|---|---|
| Type | `numeric` |
| Grain | `rate` |
| Unit | `units per week` — fixed |
| Added by | `20260614000001_item_master.sql` |
| Read by the engine | `project_map.py::_map_supply -> per-supplier capacity` |
| Transform | passed through as None when NULL; None means no capacity constraint |
| When NULL, the engine uses | unlimited |
| Validated at ingest | numeric > 0 when present |
| Rendered at | *not yet recorded (WP 5.1)* |

**The engine calls this `defaulted`.** Empty means unlimited (a valid modeling choice) — but partial-magnitude supplier disruptions need a finite capacity to throttle, else they degrade to full outages.

Fallback chain, from the engine's own registry: none — the absence is the value.

| When | The value used | Shown as | Visible where |

| NULL | unlimited capacity | `default` | the grid renders it as 0 with no dot — which is D17, and wrong |

**Resolution** — how a value is decided when more than one source could supply one.

| | |
|---|---|
| Default mode | `asserted` |
| Assertable by | `csv_upload`, `item_master_form` |
| Estimable from | **never** — this value may not be estimated |
| Hybrid (centre / spread) | **none** — the engine has no variability field for this quantity |
| On conflict | `assertion_wins` |

estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. Capacity is what the supplier CAN ship, not what they HAVE shipped. Estimating it from delivery history caps it at observed demand, so a capacity constraint fitted this way can never bind and can never explain a shortage — which is precisely the question it exists to answer. NULL continues to mean unlimited; that is an assertion too.

> D17 lives here. NULL means unlimited, but the grid's liveDefault is `derivedVal ?? 0`, so an unlimited supplier renders as a capacity of ZERO with provenance `default` — whose colour is null, so there is no dot to question. The grid states the opposite of what the model means. WP 6.2 fixes it.
